query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated atomistic simulation framework that independently models DFT-based electron transport and ML-trained phonon transport—calibrated to include defect and oxygen impurity effects—will predict the thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr with an error reduction from approximately 30% (typical of existing, convolved models) to about 10%, by accurately decoupling lattice and electronic contributions.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with ~1 wt.% oxygen impurities, featuring significant atomic-scale lattice distortions and variations in interatomic force constants.
generation.intervention: Implementation of an integrated simulation approach combining DFT-derived electronic transport calculations with machine-learned interatomic potentials for phonon (lattice) transport, explicitly calibrated for defect and impurity effects.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted in two regimes: below 200 K, where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable, and at 300–1200 K, consistent with experimental measurements on oxygen-containing specimens.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale lattice distortions and defect scattering induced by oxygen impurities, which affect the force constant variations and mass disorder in the alloy.
generation.mechanism: By decoupling the two heat transport channels, the model isolates the separate scattering mechanisms: electron scattering (from impurity and lattice disorder) and phonon scattering (due to mass and force constant variations). This separation facilitates independent calibration and improved combined prediction of the total thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivities that, when summed, yield a total thermal conductivity matching experimental observations (approximately 10–17 W/(K m) at high temperatures), with an overall error margin reduced to around 10% relative to earlier combined approaches.
generation.baseline: Prior approaches that either use simplified analytical models (e.g., based on Debye temperature approximations) or simulations assuming defect‐free crystals, which typically show error margins near 30% and fail to separately account for lattice and electronic contributions in oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr.
generation.boundary: The model predictions are applicable only to bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples containing roughly 1 wt.% oxygen within the studied temperature ranges (T < 200 K and 300–1200 K). Predictions may not extend to significantly different impurity levels or microstructural variations.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the precise quantification of the error reduction due to potential complexities in accurately modeling defect scattering and electron–phonon coupling in the presence of oxygen. Further experimental calibration is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with ~1 wt.% oxygen and perform thermal conductivity measurements in two regimes: (1) below 200 K, using techniques (e.g., magnetic field modulation) to separately resolve lattice and electronic contributions, and (2) from 300 to 1200 K to obtain total conductivity. Compare experimental findings with the predictions from the integrated simulation framework.
measurements: Separate lattice and electronic thermal conductivity at T < 200 K
Total thermal conductivity at T = 300–1200 K
Error analysis comparing predicted and measured values (targeting an error reduction from ~30% to ~10%)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulation framework does not yield separate lattice and electronic conductivity values that, when combined, reproduce experimental measurements within an error margin reduced by at least 20% (i.e., from ~30% to ~10%), or if the predicted total thermal conductivity falls outside the 10–17 W/(K m) range at high temperatures, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractLattice distortions are intrinsic features of all solid solution alloys associated with varying atomic radii; this phenomenon facilitates the formation of single-phase solid solutions. Using high-entropy alloys (HEAs), as an example, we investigate the influence of variations in inter-atomic separations for stabilizing and controlling their structural, mechanical, and thermodynamic properties. This is done through a combination of statistical mechanics analysis and molecular dynamics simulations on simplified 2D systems, as well as a 3D crystals with harmonic and anharmonic inter-atomic bonds with varying natural inter-atomic separations. We demonstrate that the impact of this inter-atomic length disorder (representing static lattice distortion) and temperature fluctuations (representing dynamic lattice distortion) on fundamental and universal thermodynamic, structural, and elastic characteristics are similar and can be unified through effective temperature; i.e. a scaling law for HEAs that establishes a relationship between these factors. cited_evidence.text: In summary, this study has established a conductivity model for the HEA system Nb-Mo-Ta-W, designed alloy compositions with high conductivity and wear resistance, which can be applied to enhance the atomic-level resolution and lifespan of atomic force microscope probes. By adjusting the composition, a refractory high-entropy material of Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 was endowed with both high hardness and electrical conductivity. We indicate that the conductivity of Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEAs can be modulated through the cocktail effect but tends to differ by an order of magnitude compared to linear combinations. The reasons for the decrease in conductivity are attributed to changes in the plasma frequency and relaxation time resulting from lattice distortions, alterations in the effective mass and density of free electrons, and variations in the crystalline size after the formation of HEAs.

AbstractNb-silicide based alloys could be used at T > 1423 K in future aero-engines. Titanium is an important additive to these new alloys where it improves oxidation, fracture toughness and reduces density. The microstructures of the new alloys consist of an Nb solid solution, and silicides and other intermetallics can be present. Three Nb5Si3 polymorphs are known, namely αNb5Si3 (tI32 Cr5B3-type, D8l), βNb5Si3 (tI32 W5Si3-type, D8m) and γNb5Si3 (hP16 Mn5Si3-type, D88). In these 5–3 silicides Nb atoms can be substituted by Ti atoms. The type of stable Nb5Si3 depends on temperature and concentration of Ti addition and is important for the stability and properties of the alloys. The effect of increasing concentration of Ti on the transition temperature between the polymorphs has not been studied. In this work first-principles calculations were used to predict the stability and physical properties of the various Nb5Si3 silicides alloyed with Ti. Temperature-dependent enthalpies of formation were computed, and the transition temperature between the low (α) and high (β) temperature polymorphs of Nb5Si3 was found to decrease significantly with increasing Ti content. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. In this study, three popular ML methods, namely random forest regressor, gradient boosting regressor, and decision tree regression models, were used for predicting the elastic properties of RCCAs. The ML model consists of eight different descriptors of RCCAs. GBR performs very well as compared with the other two ML models. While predicting elastic constants C11, C12, and C44, the R2 value of testing data of the GBR model were 0.97, 0.803, and 0.787, respectively. The GBR model has a high R2 value and low MAE and RMSE error than RF and XGB ML models and is promising for predicting the elastic constant of RHEAs. The elastic constants of alloys MoNbTiVZr, MoNbTiZr, NbTiVZr, and NbTaTiV predicted by the GBR model are consistent with the current simulation and experimental findings, which validate its prediction accuracy and applicability. The feature importance from SHAP and PCP plot shows that the VEC and MT are the most influential features affecting the elastic constants of RHEAs. The dataset created in this study using CALPHAD and DFT modeling could help scientists to construct RHEAs that can endure extreme temperatures and pressures. decision.trend: Early work on HEAs used analytical models founded on average material parameters (e.g., Debye temperature, atomic mass, and force constants) that assumed perfect, defect‐free crystals. This evolved into atomistic studies employing lattice dynamics, molecular dynamics simulations, and scaling laws to address the impact of chemical disorder and lattice distortions on phonon (lattice) transport. In parallel, specialized studies began to tease out electrical conduction features using low-frequency conductivity models. However, these efforts usually treated lattice and electronic contributions in isolation or merged them into a single effective parameter, thereby falling short in representing the full complexity (including defect and impurity effects) observed in real refractory HEAs such as HfNbTaTiZr.
decision.unsolved: No existing approach provides a unified atomistic framework that separately predicts lattice and electronic thermal conductivity in complex, impurity-containing refractory HEAs over both low (T < 200 K) and high (300–1200 K) temperature ranges. In particular, accurate decoupling of the two transport channels in a defective (oxygen‐bearing) matrix remains unsolved.
decision.lever: integrated atomistic simulation framework that couples DFT-based electron transport calculations with machine-learned interatomic potentials for phonon transport, explicitly calibrated to capture defect and impurity (e.g., oxygen) effects
decision.why: This next step follows the established trend from simplified Debye and defect-free DFT approaches toward more atomistically informed, multi-scale models. By decoupling electron and phonon contributions through a hybrid computational method, the predictive model can quantitatively improve accuracy (e.g., reducing error margins from ~30% to ~10%) and reliably cover the disparate temperature regimes indicated by experiments on HfNbTaTiZr. Decisive falsification would come from comparisons with low-temperature measurements (where lattice and electronic contributions are separately resolved) and high-temperature total conductivity in oxygen-containing samples.
